title: What actually saves subscribers on Apple's cancel screen? First benchmarks from 30 apps
summary: The first benchmarks for Apple's Retention Messaging API: save rates by message type and plan, whether discounts beat a good message, and how to set yours up.
body_markdown:
Apple finally gave us a seat at the cancel screen. Now we have the first numbers on what happens there.


Since Apple opened the[Retention Messaging API](https://superwall.com/docs/integrations/apple-retention-messaging) , every guide out there covers setup. Nobody has shared results. So we looked at every retention message Superwall served in production over the last 30 days, across 30 iOS apps.


## How we measured


- **Data:** every retention message Superwall served in production in the last 30 days (Aug 31 to Sep 28, 2026). That's about 73,000 sends across 30 iOS apps.
- **Message types:** text message, promotional offer, and switch-plan. These are the three responses Apple lets you return.
- **Save:** the subscriber did not cancel within 24 hours of seeing the message. This is the same definition as the Save Rate chart in the Superwall dashboard.
- **Median, not average:** a few big apps drive most of the volume. So we calculate a save rate for each app, then take the median. It tells you what a typical app sees.
- **Excluded:** apps with fewer than 100 sends of a given type, and one app whose cancellation events don't reach Superwall.


A text message and a switch-plan offer, both shown on the native iOS cancellation screen.


## The benchmark


A typical app keeps 13 to 21% of people who reach the cancel screen, depending on the message type.


Message type Apps Median save rate Middle half of apps Best app


Text message 11 20.7% 7 to 29% 45%


Promotional offer 11 17.7% 10 to 23% 30%


Switch-plan 12 12.9% 5 to 20% 28%


These numbers look low if you're used to paywall conversion rates. Remember who's on this screen: people who went into Settings to manage their subscription, and more than 80% of them cancel. Keeping 1 in 5 of them is a real win you'd otherwise never get.


## What we learned


### 1. Discounts don't clearly beat a good message


We looked at eight apps that ran both a text message and a discount (promo or switch-plan). In six of them, the text message did as well or better.


App Text message Discount


App A 20.7% 15.4% (promo)


App B 22.0% 20.4% (switch-plan)


App C 15.0% 13.4% (promo)


App D 29.3% 19.5% (switch-plan)


App E 34.3% 27.5% (switch-plan)


App F 45.3% 17.7% (promo), 14.4% (switch-plan)


App G 26.1% 29.8% (promo)


App H 7.1% 8.3% (promo)


One caveat: the biggest gaps (Apps D, E and F) come from apps with only 100 to 150 text sends. Among apps with 300+ text sends, text still won in three of five. So it's not that text always wins. It's that discounts don't reliably win.


**Which text works best?** We grouped the text messages by angle. Naming exactly what people lose came out on top.


Angle Example Apps Median save rate


Concrete loss "You'll lose your scans, scores and history" 8 21%


Lost progress or streak "Your streak ends here" 1 29%


Personal goal reminder "You wanted to work out more consistently" 2 14%


Fear of missing out "New content is added every week" 1 7%


- **Be specific.** The top messages named things the user built or owns: their scans, their library, their data. A generic "You'll lose access to the app" saved only 6%.
- **Look back, not forward.** Reminding people what they already have beat promising what's coming next.
- **Make it personal.** A goal reminder worked when it echoed the user's own goal, and fell flat as a generic pep talk.


Each message ran in a different app, so these are strong hints, not proof.


This doesn't mean discounts never work. It means you should earn the discount. Test a strong message first, then see if a promo beats it.


### 2. Switch-plan is mostly a nudge


Switch-plan had the lowest median save rate at 12.9%. And only about 1.4% of switch-plan sends ended in an actual plan change within 24 hours. Most of its saves are people who just didn't cancel.


If you use it, point people to a longer plan. Apps that offered weekly subscribers an annual plan saved 11 to 21%. Apps that offered monthly subscribers annual saved 5 to 18%.


### 3. Weekly subscribers are the hardest to keep


Plan being cancelled Apps Median save rate


Annual 19 16.3%


Monthly 9 13.5%


Weekly 8 12.6%


Our guess: annual subscribers have more to lose, so a reminder lands better. Weekly subscribers often decided long before they got to Settings.


### 4. Most saves stick


We checked the same subscribers 7 days later. Text and promo saves hold up well: median save rates drop by only 1.5 to 3 points. Switch-plan drops from 11.6% to 7.9%, so about a third of those saves cancel within the week.


## How to set yours up


Start simple, measure, then add discounts where they earn their place.


1. **Set a default message for every product and locale.** Apple shows it whenever a real-time response fails. Locales don't carry over, so en-US won't cover en-GB.
2. **Write a loss-framed message first.** You get 66 characters for the header and 144 for the body. Name the one thing people lose: progress, streaks, saved content, shared access.
3. **Match the offer to the plan.** Apple only tells you the product and locale, so segment on those. Offer weekly and monthly subscribers a switch to annual. Keep promo offers for plans where price is the obvious reason people leave.
4. **Submit early.** Every production message and image goes through Apple review, and it can take days.
5. **Rotate and compare.** Run one message type per product for a couple of weeks, swap it, and compare save rates in the Superwall dashboard. We're also working on native A/B testing for retention messages, so you'll soon be able to run this comparison automatically instead of rotating manually.


## What this data can't tell you (yet)


- **Save rate isn't lift.** Nobody runs a "no message" control, so some of these people would have stayed anyway.
- **Apps chose their own message types.** Text messages often run as the default fallback, so they reach different products and locales than offers do.
- **It's early.** 30 days of data and 30 apps. We'll update these numbers as more apps go live.
- **"Sent" means we answered Apple.** Apple doesn't confirm the message was shown on the device.

## FAQ


What's a typical save rate for Apple's Retention Messaging API? Across 30 iOS apps and 73,000 sends over 30 days, the median app saves 13 to 21% of subscribers who reach the cancel screen, depending on message type. The best apps save 25 to 30%.


Do discounts save more subscribers than a plain message? Not reliably. Across eight apps that ran both, a plain text message did as well as or better than a discount in six of them. Median save rate was 20.7% for text versus 17.7% for promotional offers. The strongest messages named exactly what the subscriber would lose.


Why does switch-plan perform worse than text or promo? Switch-plan had the lowest median save rate (12.9%), and only about 1.4% of switch-plan sends actually resulted in a plan change within 24 hours — most of its 'saves' are people who simply didn't cancel. It works best when it offers weekly or monthly subscribers a switch to annual.


Does Superwall support Apple's Retention Messaging API? Yes. Superwall hosts the Retention Messaging callback endpoint, message management, and save-rate reporting from the dashboard, with no app update or backend required. Your app still needs Apple's approval for the API first.
